concepts.name: Article 143: Constitutional Basis and Scope of Presidential Reference
key_dimensions: Exact text of Article 143(1) vs 143(2) — two distinct clauses with different obligations
Who initiates: President's discretion vs Cabinet advice under Article 74
Nature of questions referable: 'law or fact of public importance' — what qualifies
Distinction from original, appellate, and writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court

concepts.name: Advisory Opinion vs Binding Judgment: Legal Status of SC's Opinion
key_dimensions: Advisory opinions are NOT binding on the President or any court — UPSC trap on 'binding' nature
Contrast with binding precedent under Article 141
Whether lower courts are bound by advisory opinions — judicial debate
Practical political weight vs legal enforceability of the opinion

concepts.name: Article 143(1) vs Article 143(2): Mandatory vs Discretionary Opinion
key_dimensions: Under 143(1): SC 'may' report — it has discretion to decline
Under 143(2): SC 'shall' report — opinion is mandatory for pre-Constitution treaty/agreement matters
What falls under 143(2): disputes under pre-Constitution treaties excluded from Article 131
UPSC trap: which clause gives SC discretion to refuse and which does not

concepts.name: Supreme Court's Discretion to Decline a Reference
key_dimensions: SC can refuse to answer under Article 143(1) — established in Re: Kerala Education Bill (1958)
Grounds for refusal: hypothetical questions, questions involving live lis (dispute), lack of sufficient facts
SC cannot refuse under Article 143(2) — mandatory obligation
Comparison: Canadian Supreme Court's similar power and its exercise

concepts.name: Re: Delhi Laws Act Case (1951) — First Major Advisory Reference
key_dimensions: Question referred: validity of legislative delegation to executive
SC rendered opinion on delegated legislation — set foundational doctrine
Significance: established that advisory jurisdiction is a constitutional function, not judicial function
Outcome used to understand limits of delegated legislation in India

concepts.name: Re: Kerala Education Bill (1958) — Scope and Procedure of Article 143
key_dimensions: SC laid down that advisory opinion cannot be rendered on purely academic/hypothetical questions
Established that procedure resembles that of a regular hearing — amicus curiae, locus standi
Discussed whether private parties can participate in advisory proceedings
Key ratio: public importance test for admissibility of reference

concepts.name: Re: Special Courts Bill (1978) — Advisory Opinion and Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: President referred question on constitutional validity of setting up special courts
SC gave opinion upholding validity with certain conditions — advisory opinion shaped legislation
Demonstrated advisory jurisdiction as a tool for pre-legislative constitutional vetting
Distinction: advisory opinion here influenced final law — blurs line between advisory and binding

concepts.name: Re: Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1992) — Limits of Advisory Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: SC declined to answer reference as matter involved a live inter-state dispute (lis)
Reinforced: Article 143 cannot be used to bypass Article 131 (original jurisdiction) or tribunal awards
Distinction between 'question of law' and an 'active legal dispute between parties'
UPSC trap: advisory jurisdiction cannot substitute for adjudicatory jurisdiction

concepts.name: Re: Rama Krishna Dalmia (Presidential Reference on SC Judges' Age) — Procedural Aspects
key_dimensions: Highlights that advisory references can concern service conditions of constitutional functionaries
SC's internal deliberation: whether full bench or constitution bench is required
Quorum requirements for advisory opinions — not explicitly specified in Constitution
Whether dissenting opinions are permissible in advisory jurisdiction

concepts.name: Dissenting Opinions in Advisory Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Constitution does not prohibit dissent in advisory opinions
Practice: individual judges may append dissenting/concurring notes — seen in Re: Special Courts Bill
Whether dissenting opinion in advisory matter carries precedential value
Contrast with dissent in binding judgments under Article 141

concepts.name: Article 143 vs Article 131: Advisory Jurisdiction vs Original Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Article 131: exclusive original jurisdiction for disputes between States/Centre — adversarial, binding
Article 143: non-adversarial, opinion-based, initiated by President not parties
UPSC trap: inter-state water disputes cannot be referred under 143 if they are live disputes
Overlap scenario: when a constitutional question arises in both contexts — which prevails

concepts.name: Article 143 vs Article 137: Advisory Jurisdiction vs Review Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Article 137 allows SC to review its own judgments — applies to binding decisions
Whether SC can 'review' or modify its advisory opinion — constitutionally unclear
No direct provision for review of advisory opinions — practical gap
UPSC trap: review under 137 does not extend to advisory opinions

concepts.name: Locus Standi and Participation of Parties in Advisory Proceedings
key_dimensions: No lis (dispute between parties) in advisory reference — no formal petitioner/respondent
SC allows participation of interested parties, State governments, and amicus curiae
Attorney General of India plays a central role in presenting reference before SC
Whether a private citizen or NGO can intervene — practice varies, SC has wide discretion

concepts.name: Role of Attorney General of India in Article 143 References
key_dimensions: Attorney General under Article 76 — duty to appear in SC on behalf of Union
AG presents the reference and assists SC in framing precise questions
AG's opinion before reference is made — role in advising President/Cabinet
Distinction: AG argues for Union; SC independently renders opinion — not bound by AG's submissions

concepts.name: Presidential Reference as a Political Tool: Constitutional Propriety vs Misuse
key_dimensions: Examples of politically motivated references — Ayodhya reference (1993) seen as controversial
SC's refusal in Ayodhya reference: question was communally sensitive and amounted to seeking advisory on disputed facts
Debate: Does Article 143 give executive a backdoor to influence judicial agenda?
Constitutional safeguard: SC's discretion to refuse under 143(1) as a check on misuse

concepts.name: Re: Ayodhya Presidential Reference (1993) — SC's Refusal and Its Significance
key_dimensions: President referred question: whether a Hindu temple existed at Ram Janmabhoomi prior to mosque construction
SC declined: question was superfluous, communally sensitive, and would not subserve national interest
Landmark: SC used public interest and propriety test — broadened grounds for refusal beyond Re: Kerala Education Bill
UPSC trap: SC refused under 143(1) discretion — not a case where opinion was mandatory

concepts.name: Advisory Jurisdiction in Comparative Constitutional Law: India vs Other Jurisdictions
key_dimensions: Canada: Supreme Court of Canada Act provides similar reference jurisdiction — opinions held binding by convention
USA: No advisory jurisdiction — separation of powers doctrine prohibits SC from issuing advisory opinions
UK: No formal advisory jurisdiction for courts — Law Officers give legal advice to Crown
UPSC angle: India's model is closer to Canada than USA — advisory opinion is persuasive not binding

concepts.name: Constitutional Validity of Article 143 — Is Advisory Jurisdiction a 'Judicial' Function?
key_dimensions: Debate: Advisory opinions do not resolve a lis — are they a judicial or consultative function?
SC in Re: Delhi Laws Act clarified: advisory jurisdiction is a constitutional duty, distinct from judicial adjudication
Separation of powers concern: does executive seeking opinion from judiciary blur the separation?
Basic structure argument: whether advisory jurisdiction can be expanded or curtailed by Parliament

concepts.name: Framing of Questions in a Presidential Reference: Precision and SC's Power to Reformulate
key_dimensions: President frames questions for SC's opinion — vague or broadly framed questions create interpretive issues
SC has power to reformulate, reframe, or limit the scope of questions referred
SC can decline to answer parts of a reference that are vague, hypothetical, or lack public importance
Practical example: In Re: Special Courts Bill, SC reframed questions for clearer constitutional analysis

concepts.name: Article 143 and Federal Implications: References Involving Centre-State Disputes
key_dimensions: President can refer questions affecting federal balance — e.g., legislative competence, concurrent list disputes
States' role in advisory proceedings — they can be heard even if not 'parties'
Advisory opinions on Centre-State fiscal matters: can they pre-empt Finance Commission recommendations?
UPSC trap: advisory opinion cannot override a statutory arbitration or tribunal award in federal disputes
